body:
Should there be a requirement about the proper usage of MAC (in contrast to digital signatures). In particular, if there are more than two participants, MAC is usually not safe.

See for example [Differences between Digital Signatures and MACs](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7515#section-10.5) in the JWS RFC (emphasis mine):

> Both signatures and MACs provide for integrity checking -- verifying that the message has not been modified since the integrity value was computed.  However, MACs provide for origination identification only under specific circumstances.  It can normally be assumed that a private key used for a signature is only in the hands of a single entity (although perhaps a distributed entity, in the case of replicated servers); however, a MAC key needs to be in the hands of all the entities that use it for integrity computation and checking. Validation of a MAC only provides corroboration that the message was generated by one of the parties that knows the symmetric MAC key. This means that <mark>origination can only be determined if a MAC key is known only to two entities and the recipient knows that it did not create the message</mark>.  MAC validation cannot be used to prove origination to a third party.

Note: another problematic scenario mentioned here is when a MAC-ed message send from A to B could be sent again from B to A.

comments.body: As discussed in #2375, this may not be for V6.
@randomstuff please can you confirm whether this should be tagged as https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/labels/V6 or as https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/labels/AppendixV.

This would be for V6.

The basic idea boils down to "beware of sharing the same authentication shared secret with more than two parties, maybe you should use digital signatures instead": if more than two parties (A, B, C) share the shared secret, A can spoof B on C or C on B.

Question: Is this useful to include this?

Question: How wan we formulate a requirement about this?

This feels a little too into the weeds of system implementation detail...

I feel like once we start getting into specific implementation principles it opens up a can of worms

I think this might still be an important point. This is an easy to make mistake with dramatic consequences, especially when using cryptographic tokens (such as JWTs). This could be a requirement to complement 9.1.2.
@danielcuthbert and @unprovable, any feedback on this?

This could be generalized into a requirement such as:

> Verify that cryptographic keys are only shared to components which need to use it. For example, a secret key should usually be shared between only two components and a private key should only be accessible by its user.

I don't thinks we have such a requirement. Is it missing?
Anything from 13.3?
This is related to 13.3.2 but not exactly the same thing, I think. Maybe this could be incorporated into 13.3.2.

> This feels a little too into the weeds of system implementation detail...

I think this is (can be) more an architecture/design question than an implementation detail.

In contrast, we do have requirement which are (important) implementation "details", such as 11.2.4 “Verify that all cryptographic operations are constant-time, with no 'short-circuit' operations in comparisons, calculations, or returns, to avoid leaking information.”

Proposition:

> Verify that cryptographic keys and shared secrets are only known by the entities which need them. In many cases, shared secrets must only by known by two entities and private keys must only be known by one entity.

This could go in V11.1?
Do we not already mandate protecting these keys? It seems a little redundant to write more on this. Also I am not sure how this would be verified.

The idea is not about protecting the keys but more about:

* avoid using the same shared secret between three or more entities (eg. if you are using a MAC shared secret for 3+ entities, it negatively impacts the authenticity guarantees);
* avoid patterns where A generates a private key and then give it over to B (instead, you should let B generate the private key so that A never gets to see it).

All these things you can verify based on the architecture and how the keys are exchanges communicated. Maybe you cannot guarantee that the same key is actually badly reused but you can verify that the architecture avoid this kind of patterns.

Hi @randomstuff, I thought about this more and I think that this is a question of cryptographic key management. We already have the following documentation requirement about that:

| # | Description | Level | #v5.0.be |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: |
| **11.1.1** | Verify that there is a documented policy for management of cryptographic keys and a cryptographic key lifecycle that follows a key management standard such as NIST SP 800-57. | 2 | v5.0.be-1.6.1 |

My thinking is that either we expand this requirement to be clearer or we add more content to the section. We could also leave this as an expected part of a key management standard.

What would be your proposal here @randomstuff?

I guess this could go into V11.1. I'm not certain this fits very well within "Cryptographic Inventory and Documentation" but that might work.

I would say it is important enough (and different enough from V11.1) to deserve its own requirement.
I strongly feel it is a part of key management but I would be comfortable for you to propose additional wording for there.

| # | Description | Level | #v5.0.be |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: |
| **11.1.5** | Verify that cryptographic keys and shared secrets are only known by the entities which need them. In many cases, shared secrets must only be known by two entities and private keys must only be known by one entity. | 2 | |

Sorry @randomstuff, I meant suggest a modification to 11.1.1 to cover it:

"_Verify that there is a documented policy for management of cryptographic keys and a cryptographic key lifecycle that follows a key management standard such as NIST SP 800-57. This should include ensuring that keys are not overshared (for example with more than two entities for shared secrets and more than entity for private keys.)_"

What do you think?
@tghosth, Yes, it looks good to me. 👍
